title: MCSplat: Multi-View Photometric and Geometric Consistent Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for Driving Scenes
claim: Similar reconstruction scores can hide very different underlying geometry; our method yields cleaner, more consistent structure than the baseline despite comparable metrics.
layout: 2 side-by-side columns top, banner middle, zoomed crop pairs bottom, numbered boxes link views
description: The top half has two side-by-side panels. The left panel is the baseline, UniSplat, and the right panel is Ours. Each panel shows rendered multi-camera driving views of a suburban street. Red boxes mark artifacts, with zoomed insets and a PSNR label (27.53 dB for UniSplat, 28.16 dB for Ours). A blue arrow points down to a rendering of the Gaussian geometry. The baseline geometry looks blurry and smeared, and ours looks sharper. Numbered cyan boxes mark regions in UniSplat and green boxes mark the same regions in ours. A pale banner in the middle reads 'Similar Reconstruction Results (PSNR) ≠ Similar Gaussian Geometry'. The bottom row has zoomed crop pairs of UniSplat versus Ours. They are grouped under (a) Geometry-Appearance Ambiguity in yellow and (b) Geometric Under-Constraint in lavender. The eye goes first to the PSNR labels and the banner.
caption: As shown by the comparison with UniSplat [ref], comparable PSNR can still correspond to fundamentally different Gaussian representations. MCSplat addresses (a) cross-view geometry-appearance ambiguity and (b) local geometric supervision unreliability by combining multi-view photometric canonicalization with uncertainty-aware geometric self-supervision, producing cleaner Gaussian geometry and more consistent structures in cross-camera overlap regions.
abstract: Driving-scene reconstruction via feed-forward Gaussian splatting from sparse multi-view images remains challenging due to two factors. First, cross-camera photometric inconsistency, caused by variations in exposure, ISP, and illumination, can be incorrectly absorbed into Gaussian geometry. Second, unreliable local geometric supervision arises from normal-based constraints near depth discontinuities. To address these issues, we present \textbf{MCSplat}, a multi-view consistent feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for driving scenes. MCSplat constructs a canonical appearance space from depth-guided multi-camera correspondences to decouple geometry learning from camera-specific appearance. A multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer restores raw camera appearance from canonical renderings, enabling photometric supervision without contaminating Gaussian geometry. To improve local geometric reliability, we estimate Fisher-information-based uncertainty from photometric sensitivity and use it to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and generalization across driving datasets. Geometry-oriented evaluations further reveal enhanced cross-view depth consistency and local surface-normal agreement, while qualitative results show fewer geometric artifacts and more coherent structures across overlapping views.
